## Introduction

This vignette walks through the complete water level processing pipeline using the `waterlogged` package. We use real test data from the ALBREDA RIVER station (ALBR_ST_30) as our example.

The pipeline processes raw HOBO U20 pressure logger data through these steps:

1. Read raw pressure logger files and link them to deployment metadata
2. Quality-check the barometric (air pressure) data
3. Read raw water level logger files
4. Attach the nearest barometric data to the water level data
5. Convert pressure readings (kPa) into water level (metres)
6. Run automatic quality checks on the water level data
7. Review plots and make manual corrections (ice, dry sensor, spikes)
8. Export the final clean dataset

**Why barometric data matters:** HOBO U20 loggers measure absolute pressure — that includes both the weight of water above the sensor and the weight of the atmosphere. To get just the water depth, we need to subtract the atmospheric pressure. That's why we process barometric data first.

This vignette assumes you have already installed `waterlogged` from the develop branch:

```r
install.packages("pak")
pak::pkg_install("dfo-pacific-science/waterlogged@develop")
```

## Setup

```{r setup}
library(waterlogged)
```

Define paths to the test data shipped with the package.

```{r paths}
metadata_file   <- system.file("extdata/water_level/metadata.csv", package = "waterlogged")
baro_folder     <- system.file("extdata/water_level/baro", package = "waterlogged")
level_folder    <- system.file("extdata/water_level/level", package = "waterlogged")
reference_file  <- system.file("extdata/water_level/stage_readings.csv", package = "waterlogged")
level_runs_file <- system.file("extdata/water_level/benchmarks.csv", package = "waterlogged")
```

## Bind Raw Barometric Logger Files (v0.1)

Reads all raw HOBO CSV files from the baro folder, parses them, and links each reading to its deployment in the metadata.

Raw HOBO files are individual downloads — one CSV per field visit. This step combines them into a single tidy data frame with consistent column names and deployment info attached.

How it works:

- Reads the HOBO header (row 2) to extract the serial number (SN)
- Matches the SN + timestamp window to the metadata deployments
- Renames columns to standard names (e.g., "Abs Pres kPa" → "airpress_kPa")
- Removes duplicate rows and trims data to deployment windows

Returns a list with two items: `[[1]]` = data frame of all combined readings, `[[2]]` = a quick-look plot.

```{r bind-baro}
baro_bound <- bind_hobo_files(
  path_to_raw_folder = baro_folder,
  metadata_path      = metadata_file
)

baro_data <- baro_bound[[1]]
baro_plot <- baro_bound[[2]]

cat("Baro data dimensions:", nrow(baro_data), "rows x", ncol(baro_data), "columns\n")
cat("Stations found:", paste(unique(baro_data$site_station_code), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Date range:", as.character(min(baro_data$timestamp)),
    "to", as.character(max(baro_data$timestamp)), "\n")
```

```{r bind-baro-preview}
head(baro_data)
```

```{r bind-baro-plot}
baro_plot
```

## Quality-Check All Barometric Data

Runs automatic quality checks on the barometric data and flags problematic readings.

Barometric data feeds into every water level and dissolved oxygen calculation. If the baro data has errors (spikes, flatlines, or out-of-range values), those errors will propagate into the final water levels. Cleaning baro first protects everything downstream.

What it checks:

- Pressure too high (> 105 kPa) or too low (< 85 kPa)
- Temperature outside plausible range (−40 to 50 °C)
- Sudden spikes (> 1.5 kPa jump between consecutive readings)
- Flatlines (6 or more identical readings in a row)

The function never modifies the raw data. Instead, it creates new `_adj` (adjusted) columns that start as copies of the raw values. Any values that fail a check are set to `NA` in the `_adj` column. Boolean flag columns (`OUTLIER_*`, `FLAG_*`) record exactly what was checked and changed.

```{r baro-qaqc}
baro_qc <- barometric_qaqc_all(
  baro_data         = baro_data,
  metadata_path     = metadata_file,
  pressure_low_kpa  = 85,
  pressure_high_kpa = 105,
  temp_low_limit    = -40,
  temp_high_limit   = 50,
  spike_threshold_kpa = 1.5,
  flatline_n        = 6
)

cat("Baro QAQC results:\n")
cat("  Total rows:      ", nrow(baro_qc), "\n")
cat("  Pressure outliers:", sum(baro_qc$OUTLIER_AP, na.rm = TRUE), "flagged\n")
cat("  Temp outliers:    ", sum(baro_qc$OUTLIER_AT, na.rm = TRUE), "flagged\n")
cat("  Disturbances:     ", sum(baro_qc$FLAG_DISTURBANCE, na.rm = TRUE), "flagged\n")
cat("  Flatlines:        ", sum(baro_qc$FLAG_FLATLINE, na.rm = TRUE), "flagged\n")
cat("  Raw NAs in airpress_kPa:     ",
    sum(is.na(baro_qc$airpress_kPa)), "\n")
cat("  Adjusted NAs in airpress_kPa_adj:",
    sum(is.na(baro_qc$airpress_kPa_adj)), "\n")
```

## Bind Raw Water Level Logger Files (v0.1)

Same as Step 1, but for the water level loggers instead of baro. The ALBR_ST_30 water level logger (HOBO U20, SN 20533550) was downloaded twice — once in April 2025 and once in October 2025. This step combines both downloads into one continuous record.

The water level logger measures the same physical quantity as the baro logger (absolute pressure in kPa), but because it's submerged, its readings include the pressure of the water column above it. At this stage, the column is named `waterpress_kPa` to distinguish it from the baro logger's `airpress_kPa`.

```{r bind-level}
level_bound <- bind_hobo_files(
  path_to_raw_folder = level_folder,
  metadata_path      = metadata_file
)

level_data <- level_bound[[1]]
level_plot <- level_bound[[2]]

cat("Water level data dimensions:", nrow(level_data), "rows x",
    ncol(level_data), "columns\n")
cat("Stations found:", paste(unique(level_data$site_station_code),
    collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

```{r bind-level-preview}
head(level_data)
```

```{r bind-level-plot}
level_plot
```

## Attach Barometric Data to Water Level (v0.2)

For each water level reading, finds the nearest barometric station and attaches the matching air pressure and temperature values.

To convert pressure to water depth, we need to know the atmospheric pressure at the same time. This step pairs each water level timestamp with the closest baro reading.

How "auto" selection works:

1. Calculates the geographic distance (Haversine formula) between each water level station and every barometric station in the metadata
2. Selects up to 3 nearest baro stations (within 30 km by default)
3. If multiple baro stations overlap in time, calibrates them against the closest one and combines them to fill gaps
4. Prefers the QAQC-adjusted values (`airpress_kPa_adj`) when available

New columns added: `airpress_kPa`, `airtemp_C`, `baro_site_stn_code`.

```{r attach-baro}
wl_with_baro <- add_nearest_baro(
  input_data         = level_data,
  baro_data          = baro_qc,
  metric             = "water level",
  baro_site_selection = "auto",
  metadata_path      = metadata_file
)

wl_data     <- wl_with_baro[[1]]
wl_baro_plot <- wl_with_baro[[2]]

cat("After baro attach:", nrow(wl_data), "rows x", ncol(wl_data), "columns\n")
cat("Baro station(s) used:",
    paste(unique(wl_data$baro_site_stn_code), collapse = ", "), "\n")

baro_na_count <- sum(is.na(wl_data$airpress_kPa))
cat("Timestamps with missing baro data:", baro_na_count,
    paste0("(", round(baro_na_count / nrow(wl_data) * 100, 1), "%)"), "\n")
```

Note that stations are dropped if the function can't find a baro match:

```{r baro-stations-check}
cat("Stations in level_data:", paste(unique(level_data$site_station_code), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Stations in wl_data:   ", paste(unique(wl_data$site_station_code), collapse = ", "), "\n")
```

```{r baro-plot}
wl_baro_plot
```

## Convert Pressure (kPa) to Water Level (metres) (v0.3)

Converts the raw pressure readings into actual water depth/stage in metres, using physics and a field reference measurement.

How the conversion works:

1. Calculates water density based on temperature (Kell 1975 equation)
2. Converts water pressure to a depth using: depth = pressure / (density × g)
3. Converts baro pressure to an equivalent depth the same way
4. Subtracts baro depth from water depth to get the water column height
5. Adds a constant "k" to anchor the result to a real-world reference (e.g., a staff gauge reading taken during a field visit)

The `select_measurement` parameter selects which field visit to use as the anchor point. The `reference_type` can be `"stage"` (staff gauge reading) or `"depth"` (direct depth measurement).

```{r convert-kpa-m}
converted <- convert_waterlevel_kPa_m(
  input_data       = wl_data,
  select_station   = "ALBR_ST_30",
  reference_data   = reference_file,
  reference_type   = "stage",
  select_measurement = 1,
  return_plots     = TRUE
)

site_wl <- converted$site_wl
ref_dat <- converted$ref_dat
wl_plot <- converted$wl_plot

cat("Converted data:", nrow(site_wl), "rows\n")
cat("Water level range:",
    round(min(site_wl$waterlevel_m, na.rm = TRUE), 3), "to",
    round(max(site_wl$waterlevel_m, na.rm = TRUE), 3), "metres\n")
cat("Reference measurements used:", nrow(ref_dat), "\n")
```

The interactive plot overlays the computed water level (blue line) with the field reference points (orange dots). If the logger is well-calibrated, the dots should sit on or near the line.

```{r convert-plot}
wl_plot
```

```{r convert-preview}
head(site_wl[, c("timestamp", "waterpress_kPa", "airpress_kPa",
                  "watertemp_C", "waterlevel_m", "ref_m")])
```

## Automatic Water Level QAQC

Runs automatic quality checks on the computed water level data and flags suspicious values. Even after a good conversion, the data may contain artifacts from ice formation, sensor drying out, or physical disturbances (e.g., a flood moving the logger).

What it checks:

- Negative water temperatures (< −1 °C removed; −1 to 0 °C set to 0)
- Ice conditions (water temp < 0.3 °C flagged but NOT removed)
- Step disturbances (water level jump > 0.1 m between readings)
- Dry sensor indicators (warm water temp + low pressure pattern)

**Important distinction — "flag" vs "edit":**

- `FLAG_*` columns = "we noticed something, please review" — the data is NOT changed.
- `OUTLIER_*` columns = "we changed the data" — the `_adj` value was modified (usually set to `NA`).

```{r wl-qaqc}
wl_qc <- qc_waterlevel(
  input_data     = site_wl,
  select_station = "ALBR_ST_30"
)

cat("QAQC results for ALBR_ST_30:\n")
cat("  Total rows:        ", nrow(wl_qc), "\n")
cat("  Ice flagged:       ", sum(wl_qc$FLAG_ICE, na.rm = TRUE), "readings\n")
cat("  Disturbance flagged:", sum(wl_qc$FLAG_DISTURBANCE, na.rm = TRUE), "readings\n")
cat("  Dry flagged:       ", sum(wl_qc$FLAG_DRY, na.rm = TRUE), "readings\n")
cat("  Temp outliers:     ", sum(wl_qc$OUTLIER_WT, na.rm = TRUE), "readings\n")
```

The QAQC log is stored as an attribute on the result. It records every automated action taken.

```{r qaqc-log}
qaqc_log <- attr(wl_qc, "qaqc_log")

if (!is.null(qaqc_log) && nrow(qaqc_log) > 0) {
  cat("QAQC log entries:\n")
  print(qaqc_log[, c("field", "action", "code", "ts_start", "ts_end")])
}
```

## Visual Review

Creates an interactive multi-panel plot for reviewing the data. Before making manual corrections, you need to see the data. The plot shows raw vs adjusted values with flag indicators so you can decide what needs fixing.

How to use the plot:

- Light traces = raw values (original, unmodified)
- Dark traces = adjusted values (after QAQC corrections)
- Colored markers = flag locations (ice, dry, disturbance)
- Use the range slider at the bottom to zoom in on specific periods
- Hover over points to see exact values and timestamps

This is an iterative process: view the plot, identify a problem period, apply a correction, re-plot to verify, and repeat until satisfied.

```{r visual-review, fig.height=10, fig.width=7}
plot_qaqc_timeseries(
  wl_data        = wl_qc,
  baro_data      = baro_qc,
  select_station = "ALBR_ST_30",
  static         = TRUE
)
```

## Manual Adjustments (Examples)

This section demonstrates the manual correction tools available. In a real project, you would apply these only after reviewing the plot and identifying specific problem periods.

Each function returns a new data frame — it does not modify the original. Always assign the result back to your working variable so corrections accumulate. The examples below use placeholder timestamps; in practice, you would pick these from the interactive plot.

### 8a. Remove ice-affected data (set to NA)

Sets `waterlevel_m_adj` and `watertemp_C_adj` to `NA` for a time window where ice was affecting the sensor. When ice forms around a pressure sensor, it creates artificial pressure readings that don't represent the actual water level. There's no way to correct for ice — the only option is to remove the affected readings entirely.

```{r manual-ice, eval=FALSE}
wl_qc <- adjust_logger_NA(
   input_data       = wl_qc,
   select_station   = "ALBR_ST_30",
   metric           = "waterlevel",
   reason_to_adjust = "ice",
   timestamp_start  = "2025-02-03 00:00:00",
   timestamp_end    = "2025-02-10 00:00:00",
   manual_note      = "Ice confirmed from field visit and temperature data"
)

```

Review the timeseries to see the change.

```{r visual-review2, fig.height=10, fig.width=7}
plot_qaqc_timeseries(
  wl_data        = wl_qc,
  baro_data      = baro_qc,
  select_station = "ALBR_ST_30",
  static         = TRUE
)
```

### 8b. Correct a spike / flatline (linear interpolation)

Replaces `waterlevel_m_adj` values within a time window with a straight line drawn between the start and end points. Appropriate when the spike is clearly an artifact and the true water level was likely smooth through that period.

```{r manual-spike, eval=FALSE}
wl_qc <- adjust_waterlevel_spike(
  input_data       = wl_qc,
  select_station   = "ALBR_ST_30",
  timestamp_start  = "2025-02-03 21:00:00",
  timestamp_end    = "2025-02-20 17:00:00",
  reason_to_adjust = "ice",
  manual_note      = "Interpolated across ice spike"
)

```

Review the timeseries to see the change.

```{r visual-review3, fig.height=10, fig.width=7}
plot_qaqc_timeseries(
  wl_data        = wl_qc,
  baro_data      = baro_qc,
  select_station = "ALBR_ST_30",
  static         = TRUE
)
```


### 8c. Correct a step offset (cable break / logger moved)

Applies a constant vertical shift to all data from a specific point onward, correcting for a sudden physical displacement. If the logger physically moves (e.g., a flood shifts the mounting bracket), all readings after that point are offset by a constant amount.

Here we will adjust the data to simulate a cable break on June 1st, and then show how to correct it. 

```{r simm-cable-break}
wl_qc <- wl_qc|> dplyr::mutate(waterlevel_m = dplyr::case_when(timestamp > as.POSIXct("2025-06-01 00:00:00" ,tz = "UTC") ~   waterlevel_m+4,
                                                     .default = waterlevel_m ))
wl_qc$waterlevel_m_adj <- wl_qc$waterlevel_m

plot_qaqc_timeseries(
  wl_data        = wl_qc,
  baro_data      = baro_qc,
  select_station = "ALBR_ST_30",
  static         = TRUE)

```

A cable break will appear as a sudden, constant shift upwards in waterlevel, since the logger has falled to the bottom of the water column (more water pressure above the logger). Correct it by identifying the timestamp just before the cable break as  timestamp_start ("2025-05-31 23:00:00") and the timestamp of the first erroneous water level reading as timestamp_end ("2025-06-01 00:00:00").

```{r manual-offset, eval=FALSE}
wl_qc <- adjust_WL_offset(
  input_data      = wl_qc,
  select_station  = "ALBR_ST_30",
  timestamp_end = "2025-06-01 01:00:00",
  timestamp_start   = "2025-06-01 00:00:00",
  manual_note     = "Cable break; logger found on streambed below stilling well"
)
```


Review the timeseries to see the change.

```{r visual-review4, fig.height=10, fig.width=7}
plot_qaqc_timeseries(
  wl_data        = wl_qc,
  baro_data      = baro_qc,
  select_station = "ALBR_ST_30",
  static         = TRUE)
  

```

### 8d. Multi-point drift correction

Corrects gradual sensor drift using known offsets at specific timestamps. Applies piecewise-linear interpolation between points.

```{r manual-drift, eval=FALSE}
drift_pts <- tibble::tibble(
  timestamp = c("2024-10-10 10:00:00", "2025-06-01 00:00:00"),
  drift_m   = c(0.0, 0.12)
)

wl_qc <- wl_multipoint_correction(
  input_data     = wl_qc,
  select_station = "ALBR_ST_30",
  drift_points   = drift_pts,
  manual_note    = "Drift correction based on field survey checks"
)
```

After any manual adjustments, always re-plot to verify:

```{r manual-replot, eval=FALSE}
plot_qaqc_timeseries(
  wl_data        = wl_qc,
  baro_data      = baro_qc,
  select_station = "ALBR_ST_30"
)
```

## Set Datum from Level Runs (Optional)

Converts water level from relative stage (metres above an arbitrary reference) to absolute elevation (metres above sea level) using surveyed benchmark data.

Staff gauge readings give you relative water level ("how high is the water on the gauge?"). Level runs tie that gauge to real-world elevation using surveying equipment. This step adds a `wl_elev_m` column with the absolute elevation.

Note: This function is marked as "still in testing" by the developers. It works for initial datum establishment but has limitations for multi-year reapplication.

```{r set-datum}
wl_datum <- wl_set_datum(
  input_data      = wl_qc,
  level_runs_path = level_runs_file,
  select_station  = "ALBR_ST_30"
)

head(wl_datum$wl_elev_m)
```

## Export Clean Data (v1.0)

Writes the final cleaned data to CSV files, one per station per year. This creates the deliverable output — the clean, quality-controlled water level record ready for analysis, reporting, or sharing.

What gets exported:

- `site_station_code`, `timestamp` (identifiers)
- `waterlevel_m` (raw, unmodified)
- `waterlevel_m_adj` (the final adjusted value — use this for analysis)
- `watertemp_C`, `watertemp_C_adj` (raw and adjusted temperature)
- All `FLAG_*`, `OUTLIER_*` columns (the audit trail)

Output file naming: `<output_folder>/<year>/clean/<station>_WL_<start>_<end>_v1.0.csv`

```{r export, eval=FALSE}
write_clean_data(
  input_data            = wl_qc,
  path_to_output_folder = "processed",
  metric                = "waterlevel"
)
```

## Recap

| Step | Function | Result |
|------|----------|--------|
| 1 | `bind_hobo_files()` on baro CSVs | `baro_data` (raw baro) |
| 2 | `barometric_qaqc_all()` | `baro_qc` (cleaned baro) |
| 3 | `bind_hobo_files()` on level CSVs | `level_data` (raw WL) |
| 4 | `add_nearest_baro()` | `wl_data` (WL + baro attached) |
| 5 | `convert_waterlevel_kPa_m()` | `site_wl` (kPa → metres) |
| 6 | `qc_waterlevel()` | `wl_qc` (auto QAQC'd) |
| 7 | `plot_qaqc_timeseries()` | (visual review) |
| 8 | Manual adjustments (as needed) | `wl_qc` (updated) |
| 9 | `wl_set_datum()` (optional) | (adds elevation) |
| 10 | `write_clean_data()` | CSV files on disk |

**Key columns to understand:**

- `waterlevel_m` — the raw computed water level (never modified)
- `waterlevel_m_adj` — the adjusted version (all corrections applied here)
- `FLAG_*` — "something looks off, please review" (data unchanged)
- `OUTLIER_*` — "we changed the data" (data was set to NA or corrected)

Always use `waterlevel_m_adj` for analysis. Compare it with `waterlevel_m` to see exactly what the QAQC process changed.
